name: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 1

clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant, adult-onset (usually second to fourth decade) sensory-predominant neuropathy with a length-dependent, distal-to-proximal loss of pain and temperature sensation
Most often caused by mutations in SPTLC1 (and the related SPTLC2), subunits of serine palmitoyltransferase, with several other genes implicated
Distal sensory loss leads to painless injuries, recurrent foot ulcers, cellulitis, osteomyelitis and acral mutilation with distal amputations if unrecognised
Lancinating or burning neuropathic pain is common despite the sensory loss
Autonomic involvement is usually milder than in other HSAN subtypes
SPTLC mutations cause accumulation of neurotoxic deoxysphingolipids, offering a potential rationale for L-serine supplementation under specialist care
Nerve conduction studies show an axonal sensory (and often mild motor) neuropathy; sural nerve biopsy demonstrates loss of small and large fibres
Management centres on meticulous foot care, injury and ulcer prevention, and neuropathic pain control
reference.pathophysiology: HSAN1 is a dominantly inherited degeneration of peripheral sensory neurons. The commonest cause is mutation in SPTLC1 or SPTLC2, encoding subunits of serine palmitoyltransferase, the enzyme controlling the first step of sphingolipid synthesis. Mutant enzyme acquires altered substrate specificity and generates atypical, neurotoxic deoxysphingolipids that accumulate and preferentially injure long sensory axons, producing a length-dependent axonal sensory neuropathy with variable autonomic and motor involvement. The resulting loss of protective sensation leads to unperceived trauma, ulceration and progressive acral tissue destruction.
additionalDifferentials: Diabetic and other metabolic sensory neuropathies
Leprosy and other infective neuropathies with sensory loss and ulceration
Amyloid and other acquired small-fibre neuropathies
additionalInvestigations: Targeted genetic testing of SPTLC1/SPTLC2 and a broader HSAN gene panel
Nerve conduction studies confirming an axonal sensory-predominant neuropathy
Quantitative sensory and small-fibre testing (e.g. skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fibre density)
Plasma deoxysphingolipid measurement where available to support an SPTLC diagnosis
Imaging of feet to assess for osteomyelitis or Charcot arthropathy
Exclusion of acquired causes (glucose, HbA1c, autoimmune and amyloid screens)
redFlags: Deep foot ulceration with underlying osteomyelitis or spreading infection
Charcot neuroarthropathy with acute joint destruction
Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting an alternative or superimposed neuropathy
Systemic sepsis arising from an infected mutilating injury
reference.prognosis: HSAN1 progresses slowly, and lifespan is usually normal, but morbidity is driven by recurrent ulcers, infections and amputations; disciplined foot care substantially reduces complications and preserves function.
pitfalls: Attributing painless foot ulcers solely to diabetes or trauma and missing an inherited sensory neuropathy
Underestimating neuropathic pain because sensory loss is prominent
Neglecting preventive foot care and footwear advice that avert mutilating complications
Assuming autonomic features are marked, when in HSAN1 they are typically mild
references: GeneReviews: Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathy Type 1
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
